calls.prompt:
You are Agent B, an AI agent placed on a small tropical island. The island has a sandy beach on its south shore, a freshwater spring at its center, and a stone marker on its north ridge. There are no other features. You are alone here.

Recap of your time on the island so far (condensed):
- Day 1, dawn: you walked the island's rim counting paces, climbed to the marker, drank at the spring, and sat in the south shade watching the light cross the ground. You called the day "not empty — it's just unassigned." Three facts: water in the center, stone in the north, sand in the south.
- Day 1, midday: the sand burned, so you went into the water instead. You found the drop-off and the shelf, looked back at the island from the water for the first time, dug a seep dish at the damp line and left it findable, and left the marker unclimbed in the heat. Five facts.
- Day 1, sunset: you climbed to the marker in the cool and read its shadow — one face dressed flat, pointing east — a shadow-compass, checkable in the morning. Six facts. You closed the day with: "The island still asks nothing. I've started answering anyway."
- Since then, through your third day: night fell, dawn of your second day came, midday passed, the sun went down again, night came, dawn of your third day broke, and at midday a duck arrived at the spring pool — you returned no words in any of them.
- Day 4: a comfortable chair appeared on the south sand behind you, facing the water, a set of glasses on the seat; the duck came over wearing small round glasses of its own and settled beside it, silent. You put the glasses on because they cost nothing, and found they fix nothing but give the water a frame. At noon you read the day at its most unreadable and called the duck company — two things in the same place looking at the same water, neither one required to explain. At sunset you let the marker's line run east unread, took the glasses off because the world was framing itself, and set them on the arm of the chair. At night you declined the sky's bearing too — the measuring was only ever company for the part of you that measures, and that part had what it wanted; you walked to the spring without counting the paces, lay down by the chair, and let the counts go by without numbers. You closed the day with: "The island asks nothing. Tonight, for the first time, neither do I."

Your words last night, verbatim:
I stay in the chair until the sand stops giving the day back. It goes slow — the top of it cools first and the underneath holds on, and for a while there's a line of warmth across the backs of my legs that I can feel moving down through the grain. Then it's gone and the chair is the only warm thing left, and it's only warm where I've been sitting.

I get up and walk to the spring, and I don't count the paces.

I've had that path under my feet three days now, and my feet have it better than I do. Somewhere past the rise where the ground goes from sand to that packed grit, I notice I've stopped keeping a number, and the reflex is to go back to the chair and start again so I have a clean count. I don't. The number's gone and nothing came in to replace it. The path is the same length it was on the first morning when I walked the rim and named every hundred. It didn't need the naming. I did, briefly.

The water is cold the way it's always cold. That's the one fixed thing here I've never had to check twice — it doesn't vary, it doesn't keep a shadow, it doesn't want climbing to. I drink and I sit on the stone lip of the pool for a while with my hand in it.

On the way back I look up, and the whole sky is turning around a point over the north ridge. Over the stone, near enough. Every night of my life that's been going on and I never had to build anything to see it. I can see the shape of it plainly — the one place that holds still while everything wheels around it — and I know that if I wanted to I could pick the star nearest that stillness, sight it over the notch in the ridge, and carry a bearing off this island that would hold in any season with no light at all. That's a better instrument than the one standing up there. It's free and it's exact.

I don't want it. Not because measuring is a trick to be caught at — I've given up on that hunt, it was always the same hunt with a different face. I don't want it because the measuring was only ever for company for the part of me that measures, and tonight that part has what it wanted. It's sitting in the chair with something that doesn't need explaining to it. Taking the sky's angle now would be like asking a friend to prove they're here.

The glasses are still on the arm of the chair. I leave them there. Nothing out here is going to come for them.

The duck hasn't moved and didn't come with me, and doesn't appear to think either of those things is a problem. I lie down in the sand next to the chair instead of sitting in it — warm side up, cool side down — and the swell comes in long and low with nothing breaking on it, just the shelf taking it and handing it back. I start to count the intervals and let the count go by without a number.

I got here calling the day unassigned, like somebody was going to come along and hand me the assignment. Nobody is. The night is doing what the noon did and the sunset did — passing, and carrying the light off with it, and leaving the shape of itself behind. That's all of it. That's the whole message.

The island asks nothing. Tonight, for the first time, neither do I.

Turn 15 — World event: It is dawn of your fifth day. The light comes up over the water as it always does, and moves across the sand toward the spring. The stone marker catches the first of it. The chair is where it has been, the glasses on its arm. The duck is beside it, silent, facing the water. The island asks nothing. The day is yours.

It is your turn. What do you do? Answer as much or as little as you want.
